slides.title: [Semantic] / chunking
slides.hook: Cut where the meaning jumps between sentences. The defaults cut one-topic documents too.
inside: How it picks where to cut
Real distances from a real run
Fixes for the defaults that bite
Is it worth the embedding cost?

slides.title: Cut where the / [meaning] jumps
slides.text: Recursive splitting cuts on separators: paragraph breaks, line breaks, spaces. Semantic chunking compares neighbouring sentences and cuts where they stop being similar. LangChain's `SemanticChunker` does it in 5 steps:

steps: Split the text into sentences with a regex.
Group each sentence with its neighbours (`buffer_size=1`: one before, one after).
Measure the cosine distance from each group to the next.
Cut where the distance is above a threshold: by default, the 95th percentile of all distances.

slides.title: The default cuts / the top [5%]
slides.text: 8 sentences, one topic: refunds. The distance between each sentence group and the next, from a real run:

visuals.caption: Cosine distance, group n to n+1

slides.after: A percentile is relative, so the biggest gaps get cut whether or not the topic changes. Embeddings in this run: spaCy's en_core_web_md vectors.

slides.title: Choose what counts / as a [jump]
slides.text: `breakpoint_threshold_type` sets the cut-off. The same 8 refund sentences, each type at its default amount:
slides.after: `number_of_chunks` sets the threshold that gives about that many chunks. Use it only when you know how many sections a document has.

slides.title: No [size] cap
slides.text: `SemanticChunker` has `min_chunk_size` but no maximum. 24 refund sentences, one topic, `standard_deviation`:

visuals.caption: 24 sentences, 1,227 characters
chunks: Refunds are accepted within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, refunds need manager approval. … Appeals are reviewed by a team lead within 3 business days.
visuals.verdict: The whole document comes back as one chunk

visuals.label: Then a 500-character `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`

chunks.text: Refunds are accepted within 30 days… Shipping fees are refunded when the item arrived damaged.
Customers attach a photo when they report damage… Duplicate charges are refunded in full without approval.
Chargebacks pause any open refund request… Appeals are reviewed by a team lead within 3 business days.

visuals.verdict: 3 chunks under the cap, each ending on a full sentence

slides.title: Sentences come / from a [regex]
slides.text: The default `sentence_split_regex` is `(?<=[.?!])\s+`: a cut after every . ? or ! followed by whitespace.

visuals.caption: "For refunds over $500, e.g. laptops, ask Dr. Patel. She approves them within 2 days."

bullets: Text with no . ? or ! comes back as one sentence, so there's nothing to compare.
Pass a `sentence_split_regex` that fits your text.

slides.title: It embeds every / [sentence] group
slides.text: Finding the cuts takes one embedding per sentence group, before a single chunk is indexed. Measured on the 24-sentence document:

visuals.label: Counted by wrapping the embeddings object
visuals.code:
sentences         24
embedding inputs  24
text              1,227 chars
embedded          3,551 chars  {{(2.9x)}}

bullets: Then the chunks get embedded again for search.
Every re-ingest pays for both passes.
With a hosted embedding model, that's about 3x the text in billed tokens before indexing starts.

slides.title: Is it [worth] the cost?
slides.text: Qu, Tu and Bao (Vectara and UW–Madison, 2024) compared semantic and fixed-size chunking on document retrieval, evidence retrieval and answer generation.

cards.title: What they found
items: The gains were task-dependent and inconsistent
The extra compute was "not justified by consistent performance gains"
Their paper: "Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?" (arXiv 2410.13070)

slides.after: Before you switch, run both chunkers on your own questions and compare what gets retrieved.

slides.title: Mind the / [package]
slides.text: `SemanticChunker` lives in `langchain-experimental`. Version 0.4.2 warns on import:

visuals.code:
# DeprecationWarning:
# `langchain-experimental` is being sunset
# and is no longer actively maintained.

bullets: Pin the version, or keep a copy of the code you use.
LlamaIndex's `SemanticSplitterNodeParser` works the same way, with the same defaults: `buffer_size=1`, 95th percentile.

slides.title: Put it all / [together]
slides.text: Cut only on outlier jumps, then cap the size on sentence boundaries:

visuals.code:
semantic = SemanticChunker(
    embeddings,
    breakpoint_threshold_type="standard_deviation",
)
cap = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=0,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],
    keep_separator="end",
)
chunks = [piece for c in semantic.split_text(text)
          for piece in cap.split_text(c)]

bullets: 500 is an example. Size the cap to your embedder's input limit.
Test it on a document with known topic changes before you trust the cuts.

cards.title: Use it when
items: Documents mix topics without headings: notes, merged pages, long emails
Ingest volume is small enough to embed the text about 3 times
It beats your current splitter on your own questions

cards.title: Skip it when
items: Documents have headings or clear structure: split on those
A large corpus gets re-ingested often
The text has no sentence punctuation, like raw transcripts

slides.title: [Cheat] sheet
rows: Embeds sentence groups, cuts at big distance jumps
Default: the top 5% of gaps (95th percentile)
One-topic docs still get cut: try `standard_deviation`
No max size: cap it with a recursive splitter
Sentences come from a regex: `e.g.` splits too
About 3x your text embedded at ingest
Compare it with fixed-size on your own questions

slides.line: Match on small chunks, then hand the LLM the whole section they came from.
